summary: Defines a flexible way to support Differentiated Services over MPLS networks. It is a standards-track document.

plainLanguage.summary: Diff-Serv gives packets different forwarding treatment, but an MPLS router may not see the IP marking that selects that treatment. RFC 3270 defines two ways to carry the needed information in MPLS labels and headers.

questions: what is an e-lsp in mpls
what is the difference between e-lsp and l-lsp
how does diffserv work over mpls
subtitle: How MPLS label-switched paths carry Differentiated Services traffic classes.

tldr.problem: Diff-Serv routers use packet markings to choose treatment, while MPLS routers forward using labels and may not see the IP header.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 3270 defines E-LSPs, which use the 3-bit EXP field to identify treatment, and L-LSPs, which infer the scheduling class from the label. RSVP and LDP extensions can signal the needed mapping.
tldr.outcome: The design lets an operator map traffic classes to one or more LSPs for forwarding and traffic engineering. RFC 3270 updates RFC 3032 and is updated by RFC 5462.

today: RFC 3270 is a Proposed Standard. It updates RFC 3032 and is itself updated by RFC 5462.

sections.title: Why MPLS Needs Diff-Serv Information
sections.content:
In a Differentiated Services (Diff-Serv) domain, packets with the same treatment form a Behavior Aggregate (BA). A router uses the packet's Diff-Serv Code Point (DSCP) to choose a Per-Hop Behavior (PHB), including scheduling treatment and, in some cases, drop probability.

A Multiprotocol Label Switching (MPLS) Label Switch Router (LSR) forwards using a label, so the Internet Protocol (IP) header may not be visible. RFC 3270 defines how an LSR identifies the treatment for a packet and encodes the needed information for the next LSR. It describes unicast operation for IPv4 and IPv6.
sections.plainLanguage: Packets can need different treatment, such as different scheduling or drop choices. MPLS routers need another way to identify that treatment when they forward by labels.

sections.title: Two Types of Label-Switched Paths
sections.content:
An EXP-Inferred-PSC Label Switched Path (E-LSP) can carry up to eight Behavior Aggregates (BAs) for a given Forwarding Equivalent Class. The 3-bit EXP field in the MPLS shim header selects the Per-Hop Behavior (PHB), including its scheduling class and drop precedence. The mapping from EXP values to PHBs is signaled during setup or configured in advance.

A Label-Only-Inferred-PSC Label Switched Path (L-LSP) carries one Ordered Aggregate for a Forwarding Equivalent Class. The label identifies its PHB Scheduling Class (PSC); drop precedence is carried in the EXP field or a link-layer field. A network may use either type or both, subject to restrictions for some link types.
sections.plainLanguage: An E-LSP uses bits in the packet to identify its treatment and can carry several behavior aggregates. An L-LSP uses its label to identify the scheduling class and carries drop precedence separately.

sections.title: The LSR Forwarding Steps
sections.content:
The RFC describes Diff-Serv forwarding in four stages. The LSR determines the incoming PHB, may condition traffic and choose an outgoing PHB, selects a label-forwarding entry, then encodes Diff-Serv information in the outgoing encapsulation. Depending on the link, that information can be in the MPLS EXP field, ATM CLP, Frame Relay DE, or 802.1 User_Priority.

The model describes behavior rather than requiring a particular implementation. Each label has a Diff-Serv context that identifies the LSP type, supported PHBs, and mappings between encapsulation values and PHBs. If a label has several possible next hops, the LSR must select one whose context supports the packet's outgoing PHB.
sections.plainLanguage: The router identifies a packet's treatment, selects a next hop, and writes the treatment information into the outgoing packet. A possible next hop must support that treatment.

sections.title: Diff-Serv Tunneling Models
sections.content:
The RFC defines the Pipe, Short Pipe, and Uniform models for Diff-Serv information across an LSP. In the Pipe model, the egress applies treatment using the outer LSP information and then removes that outer label; this model requires operation without Penultimate Hop Popping (PHP). The Pipe model must be supported.

The optional Short Pipe model applies egress treatment using the tunneled information and can operate with or without PHP. The optional Uniform model treats MPLS as transparent to Diff-Serv: the meaningful information remains in the outermost label entry, or in the IP header when the packet leaves unlabelled. For each LSP level, the ingress and the node that pops its label must use the same model.
sections.plainLanguage: The three models define which Diff-Serv marking controls treatment at the end of an LSP. Pipe uses the outer marking, Short Pipe uses the tunneled marking at the egress, and Uniform carries one meaningful marking through the path.

sections.title: Signaling LSP Type and Mappings
sections.content:
The Resource ReSerVation Protocol (RSVP) can carry an optional DIFFSERV object in a Path message. Its class is 65. C-Type 1 identifies an E-LSP and can carry MAP entries that associate EXP values with PHB identifiers; C-Type 2 identifies an L-LSP and carries its PSC. An E-LSP with a preconfigured mapping can be requested without MAP entries.

The Label Distribution Protocol (LDP) can carry an optional Diff-Serv Type Length Value (TLV), type 0x0901, in label request and mapping messages. Its T bit distinguishes E-LSP from L-LSP; the TLV carries either the mapping entries or the PSC. The RFC also defines RSVP Diff-Serv error code 27 and corresponding error values for unsupported or invalid requests.
sections.plainLanguage: RSVP and LDP messages can tell neighboring routers which kind of LSP to create. They can also carry the mapping or scheduling class the routers need to use.

sections.title: Restrictions on Link Types
sections.content:
On PPP, LAN, and non-label-controlled ATM and Frame Relay interfaces, a Diff-Serv LSR must support E-LSPs that use a preconfigured mapping; support for signaled E-LSPs and L-LSPs is optional. On label-switching-controlled ATM and Frame Relay interfaces, E-LSPs are not supported, so the LSR must support L-LSPs.

The RFC does not select ATM service categories or Frame Relay parameters. It requires forwarding behavior to follow the relevant PHB specifications.
sections.plainLanguage: Which LSP types are available depends on the link. The RFC requires L-LSP support on label-controlled ATM and Frame Relay links, where E-LSPs are not supported.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content:
The RFC allocates RSVP class number 65 for the DIFFSERV object and error code 27 for Diff-Serv errors. It defines error values 1 through 5 for that code. It also defines an LDP Diff-Serv TLV and five Diff-Serv-related LDP status codes.

The RFC specifies that future RSVP error values use First Come First Served allocation. The new LDP values follow the allocation policies of LDP.
sections.plainLanguage: The document assigns numbers for RSVP objects and errors, plus an LDP type and status codes. It also states how future RSVP error values are allocated.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC says it introduces no new security issues beyond those inherent in Diff-Serv, MPLS, and RSVP. It may use the same security mechanisms proposed for those technologies.
sections.plainLanguage: The authors identify no security issues beyond those already associated with Diff-Serv, MPLS, and RSVP.
